label: def:contraction-routine
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:contraction-routine}
Consider an optimization subroutine
$
\mathsf{Contract}(y,R;\mathrm{SO}_\lambda),
$
which takes an initial point $y$, a target radius $R$, and a stochastic oracle $\mathrm{SO}_\lambda$ as inputs. Associated with the subroutine are a bias-admissibility condition $\mathsf{Adm}_{\rm C}(R,\mathcal{B}_\lambda)$ and an oracle complexity bound $T(R,\lambda)$.
          
    
                                      
                 
               
    
We say that $\mathsf{Contract}$ is a valid distance-contraction subroutine if, whenever
\[
\mathbb{E}\|y-x^*\|^2\le R^2
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathsf{Adm}_{\rm C}(R,\mathcal{B}_\lambda)\text{ holds},
\]
it uses at most $T(R,\lambda)$ calls to $\mathrm{SO}_\lambda$ and returns $y^+$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}\|y^+-x^*\|^2\le \frac{R^2}{2}.$
head: environment
name: Distance-contraction subroutine

label: prop:known-restart
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:known-restart}
Suppose $\mathbb{E}\|y^0-x^*\|^2\le R_0^2$ and the admissible set $\ensuremath{\mathcal{P}}_s$ in Algorithm~\ref{alg:known} is nonempty at every completed stage. Then
\[
    \mathbb{E}\|y^s-x^*\|^2\le R_s^2=2^{-s}R_0^2.
\]
Consequently, after $K=\lceil\log_2(R_0^2/\epsilon)\rceil$ stages, we have
$\mathbb{E}\|y^K-x^*\|^2\le\epsilon$.
head: environment
name: Stagewise convergence

title: Proof
body_md:
The claim follows by induction. At stage $s$, the selected oracle $\lambda_s$ is admissible, so Definition~\ref{def:contraction-routine} guarantees
$
\mathbb{E}\|y^s-x^*\|^2\le R_{s-1}^2/2=R_s^2.
$
head: environment

label: thm:sge
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Biased SGE

title: Proof sketch
body_md:
To prove the claim, we need to control the state-dependent
variance, and also bound the error introduced by the persistent
oracle bias. We begin with the SGE recursion stated in Proposition \ref{prop:general_convergence}, whose proof follows from a similar analysis of SGE as in \cite{ilandarideva2025state} (see Appendix \ref{subsec:proof_of_proposition}).
With this recursion, we can handle the state-dependent variance and systematic bias transparently. Our parameter choices ensure that the state-dependent variance
terms can be absorbed into the converging function-value terms in this
recursion. Taking the telescoping sum over the recursions yields
\[
A_k \mathbb{E}[f(x_k)-f^\ast]
+\frac{P_k}{2}\mathbb{E}\|z_k-x^\ast\|^2
\leq
\Gamma_k+B\sum_{t=1}^k(3t-2)\mathbb{E}\|z_t-x^\ast\|,
\]
where $A_k$ and $P_k$ grow quadratically in $k$, and $\Gamma_k$
contains the initial-error and residual-variance terms. To bound the accumulated bias, observe that the same inequality
controls the distance of each $z_t$ from $x^\ast$. Thus, the
distances appearing on the right-hand side can themselves be
bounded in terms of the accumulated error. Applying Young's
inequality provides a bound of the form
$2\Gamma_k+O(k^2B^2/\mu)$, and dividing both sides of the inequality by $A_k$ yields the stated
function-value bound. By further using the strong convexity property, we can obtain the
distance-contraction guarantee. The full proof is deferred to Appendix~\ref{sec:proof_sge_thm}.\qed
head: manual
name: sketch

label: corollary_known
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Comparison with the best fixed oracle

title: Proof sketch
body_md:
The comparison with the best fixed oracle follows directly
from minimizing the cost at each stage: the sum of the
stagewise minima is no larger than the minimum of the sums.
It remains to show how large this improvement can be.

We first construct two oracles. The first has a smaller
coarse-scale cost but a larger residual-variance term, whereas
the second has a constant stage cost of $M$ throughout the
optimization horizon. The parameters are chosen so that the
first oracle is cheaper until the final
$m=\lceil\log_2 K\rceil$ stages. Thus, the adaptive policy
incurs a total cost of $\Theta(M\log K)$, while the best
fixed oracle incurs a cost of $MK$.

To show that this order cannot be improved, let $d_s$ denote
the minimum cost at stage $s$, and consider an oracle attaining
$d_{K-m}$. Its cost over all $K$ stages is at most
$O(Kd_{K-m})$. On the other hand, because $d_s$ is
nondecreasing, the adaptive policy pays at least
$(m+1)d_{K-m}$ over the final $m+1$ stages. Combining these
bounds gives an improvement of at most $O(K/\log K)$.
The construction with tight examples, and the complete bounds are presented
in Appendix~\ref{proof_corollary_known}. \qed
head: manual
name: sketch

label: rem:domination
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:domination}
Oracle $\nu$ dominates oracle $\lambda$ if
\[
\mathcal{B}_\nu\le\mathcal{B}_\lambda,
\quad
c_\nu D_\nu\le c_\lambda D_\lambda,
\quad
c_\nu\sigma_{\nu,*}^2\le c_\lambda\sigma_{\lambda,*}^2.
\]
Then $\nu$ is admissible whenever $\lambda$ is, and $C_\nu(R)\le C_\lambda(R)$ for every $R$; hence Algorithm~\ref{alg:known} with SGE subroutine never selects $\lambda$.
head: environment
name: Domination

title: Remark
body_md: We analyze exact trusted-gradient certification in order to isolate this certification-frequency tradeoff from the statistical problem of constructing the certificate itself. In applications, the certification module $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ may instead be constructed using a sufficiently large trusted sample, expert-reviewed observations, or repeated measurements. Standard concentration arguments can then construct a high-probability confidence bound for the projected-gradient norm. We leave the joint tradeoff among trusted-sample size, statistical precision, and certification frequency for a stochastic certification oracle to future work.

head: environment
name: Projected-gradient certificate

label: def:pg-reduction-routine
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:pg-reduction-routine}
Consider a subroutine
$
\mathsf{PGReduce}(y,R;\mathrm{SO}_\lambda),
$
where $y$ is an initial point, $R$ is the current radius, and $\mathrm{SO}_\lambda$ is the stochastic oracle used for training. Associated with the subroutine are a bias-admissibility condition $\mathsf{Adm}_{\rm PG}(R,\mathcal{B}_\lambda)$ and a known oracle complexity $\widetilde T(R,\lambda)$.
    
                                       
       
                          
    
We say that $\mathsf{PGReduce}$ is valid if, whenever
\[
\mathbb{E}\|y-x^*\|^2\le R^2
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathsf{Adm}_{\rm PG}(R,\mathcal{B}_\lambda)\text{ holds},
\]
it uses at most $\widetilde T(R,\lambda)$ oracle calls to $\mathrm{SO}_\lambda$ and returns a candidate $y^+\in X$ satisfying
\[
   \mathbb{E}\|\mathsf{G}_{X}(y^+)\|\le \tfrac{\sqrt{2}\mu R}{16}.
\]
head: environment
name: Projected-gradient reduction subroutine

label: lem:block-validity
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Validity of an admissible block

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $u_s:=y^s$, thus $\|u_s-x^*\|^2\le R_s^2.$ For $k=s,\ldots,t-2$ define
\[
u_{k+1}
:=
\mathsf{Contract}(u_k,R_k;\mathrm{SO}_\lambda).
\]
By Definition~\ref{def:contraction-routine} and the contraction-admissibility conditions in \eqref{eq:block-admissibility}, a simple induction implies
\[
\mathbb{E}\|u_k-x^*\|^2\le R_k^2,
\quad \text{for }
k=s,\ldots,t-1.
\]
Therefore, the input $u_{t-1}$ to the terminal projected-gradient reduction satisfies the mean-square warm-start condition at radius $R_{t-1}$. Definition~\ref{def:pg-reduction-routine} and the terminal PG-admissibility condition then imply \eqref{eq:block-expected-pg}. By applying Markov's inequality, we have
\[
\ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}\left(
\|\mathsf{G}_X(z)\|>
\tfrac{\sqrt{2}\mu R_{t-1}}{4}
\right)
\le
\tfrac{
\mathbb{E}\|\mathsf{G}_X(z)\|
}{
\sqrt{2}\mu R_{t-1}/4
}
\le \tfrac14,
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:block-success}.
head: environment

label: prop:sequential-block-cert
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Sequential certification

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:block-validity}, every independent block trial succeeds with probability at least $3/4$. Hence the probability that the first $r$ trials all fail is at most $4^{-r}$. Therefore
\[
\ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}(\text{the block certification fails})
\le 4^{-\mathcal R}.
\]
The expectation for the total number of trials for a successful certification is bounded by
\[
\mathbb{E}[N]
=
\sum_{r=0}^{\mathcal R-1}\ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}(N>r)
\le
\sum_{r=0}^{\mathcal R-1}4^{-r}
\le
\tfrac43,
\]
which completes the proof.
head: environment

label: prop:budgeted-correctness
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:budgeted-correctness}
Let
$
K=\lceil\log_2(R_0^2/\epsilon)\rceil
$
and choose
$
\mathcal R
\ge
\left\lceil
\log_4\frac{K+\ell}{\delta}
\right\rceil.
$
Suppose that whenever Algorithm~\ref{alg:budgeted-certification} has not yet reached certified level $K$, the current pool contains at least one oracle that is block-admissible. 
                                    
Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$, the algorithm terminates with a certified point $y$ satisfying
$
\|y-x^*\|^2\le\epsilon.
$
                                                                                          
The total number of blocks is bounded by
$K+\ell = O\!\left(
\ell+\log\tfrac{R_0^2}{\epsilon}
\right),
$
and the number of trusted-gradient evaluations is at most
\[
O\!\left\{
\left(
\ell+\log\tfrac{R_0^2}{\epsilon}
\right)
\log\!\left(
\tfrac{\ell+\log(R_0^2/\epsilon)}{\delta}
\right)
\right\}.
\]
head: environment
name: High-probability convergence guarantee of budgeted certification

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider a block-admissible oracle. By Lemma~\ref{lem:block-validity}, one independent block trial fails to certify the full target with probability at most $1/4$. Therefore all $\mathcal R$ independent trials fail with probability at most
$
4^{-\mathcal R}\le\tfrac{\delta}{K+\ell}.
$
Every fully successful block advances the certified level by at least one, so there can be at most $K$ such blocks. Every unsuccessful block permanently removes one oracle, so there can be at most $\ell$ unsuccessful blocks. A union bound over at most $K+\ell$ block decisions shows that, with probability at least $1-\delta$, no block-admissible oracle is incorrectly removed.

Every advancement of the certified level, whether a full-block success or the partial progress, is justified by the exact projected-gradient certificate in Lemma~\ref{lem:pg-certificate}. Thus the certified state always satisfies
$
\|y^s-x^*\|^2\le R_s^2.
$
Under the stated availability condition, an unfinished level cannot exhaust all block-admissible oracles on the above high-probability event. Thus the certified level eventually reaches $K$, where
$
R_K^2\le\epsilon.
$

Finally, each certification round queries the trusted certification module at most $\mathcal{R}$ times. Multiplying $\mathcal{R}$ by $K + \ell$ yields the stated trusted-gradient complexity.

label: thm:rr-sge-subroutine
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: RR+SGE projected-gradient reduction

title: Proof
body_md:
We next work toward proving Theorem~\ref{thm:rr-sge-subroutine}. 
Throughout the proof, define
\[
    x_j^*\in\arg\min_{x\in Y}\phi_j(x),
    \quad
    \phi_j^*=\phi_j(x_j^*),
\]
and let
\[
    \ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_j(x,\xi)
    =
    \ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}(x,\xi)
    +
    \sum_{i=1}^j\rho_i(x-\widehat x_i),
    \quad
    g_j(x)
    =
    g(x)
    +
    \sum_{i=1}^j\rho_i(x-\widehat x_i).
\]
Note that the original oracle satisfies
$
    \|g(x)-\nabla f(x)\|_*
    \le \mathcal{B},
$
and
                                
\begin{align}
    \mathbb{E}\|\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}(x,\xi)-g(x)\|_*^2
    \le
    \ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}(f(x)-f^*)+\sigma_*^2.
    \label{assump:state-dependent}
\end{align}
The first lemma shows that recursive regularization preserves the oracle bias and the state-dependent form of its variance.

\begin{lemma}[State-dependent noise under recursive regularization]
\label{lem:rr-noise}
     
   
               
   
                   
    
               
       
                   
       
                                           
                   
    
       
    
                        
    
suppose
$
    \mathbb{E}\bigl[
      \phi_{j-1}(\widehat x_j)-\phi_{j-1}^*
    \bigr]
    \le \delta_j.
$
Then the bias satisfies
\[
    \|g_j(x)-\nabla\phi_j(x)\|_*
    \le \mathcal{B}.
\]
Moreover, conditioned on the previous recursive-regularization
iterates, the state-dependent variance satisfies
\[
    \mathbb{E}\|\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_j(x,\xi)-g_j(x)\|_*^2
    \le
    \ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}\bigl(\phi_j(x)-\phi_j^*\bigr)
    +\widehat\sigma_{j,*}^2,
\]
where
$
    \widehat\sigma_{j,*}^2
    :=
    \sigma_*^2
    +
    \ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}
    \sum_{i=1}^j
    \tfrac{\rho_i}{2}
    \|x_{i-1}^*-\widehat x_i\|^2.
$
In particular, $
    \mathbb{E}[\widehat\sigma_{j,*}^2]
    \le
    \sigma_*^2
    +
    \ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}\sum_{i=1}^j\delta_i.
$
\end{lemma}
We defer the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:rr-noise} to Appendix~\ref{proof:lem:rr-noise}.

The second ingredient is the deterministic RR reduction: sufficiently accurate solutions of the regularized subproblems imply a small projected-gradient mapping for the original objective.

\begin{proposition}[Recursive-regularization reduction; cf.~\citet{allen2018gradient,foster2019complexity}]
\label{prop:rr-pg}
Let $S
    :=
    1+\left\lceil\log_2\tfrac{L}{\mu}\right\rceil$, 
    $
    \rho_j:=2^{j-1}\mu.
$
For $j=1,\ldots,S$, suppose $\widehat x_j$ is an approximate
minimizer of $\phi_{j-1}$ over $X$ satisfying
$
    \mathbb{E}[
       \phi_{j-1}(\widehat x_j)-\phi_{j-1}^*
    ]
    \le\delta_j.
$
Then, with $
    \gamma=\frac{1}{2L},
$
the final point $\widehat x_S$ satisfies
\begin{align}
    \mathbb{E}\|\mathsf{G}_{X}(\widehat x_S)\|
    \le
    (2+\sqrt{2})\sum_{j=1}^{S-1}\sqrt{\rho_j\delta_j}
+
6\sqrt{\rho_S\delta_S}.
\label{eq:RR_reduction}
\end{align}
\end{proposition}
The proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:rr-pg} follows from the analysis techniques in \citet{allen2018gradient,foster2019complexity}. For the sake of completeness, we provide a complete proof in Appendix~\ref{proof:prop:rr-pg}.

head: environment
name: Recursive-regularization reduction

label: eq:cert-delta-choice
title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{proof}
For a sufficiently small universal constant $a>0$, set
\begin{equation}
    \delta_j
    :=
    \tfrac{a\mu^2R^2}{S^2\rho_j},
    \quad
    \rho_j=2^{j-1}\mu,
    \quad
    j=1,\ldots,S.
\label{eq:cert-delta-choice}
\end{equation}
We show that SGE can solve every recursively regularized subproblem
to the accuracy $\delta_j$ with the stated total complexity by inductive arguments.

For the first subproblem, condition on the possibly random warm start $\widehat x_0$, apply the SGE bound in Theorem~\ref{thm:sge}, and then average over $\widehat x_0$. Since
$
\mathbb{E}\|\widehat x_0-x^*\|^2\le R^2,
$
the resulting first-stage bound is identical to the deterministic-warm-start case. Applying \eqref{eq:sge-rate} with mini-batch size
$m=1$, it suffices to use
\begin{equation}
k_1
=
O\left(
S\sqrt{\tfrac{L}{\mu}}
+
\tfrac{S\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}}{\mu}
   
                          
+
\tfrac{S^2\sigma_*^2}{\mu^2R^2}
\right)
\label{eq:cert-first-budget}
\end{equation}
iterations to make all vanishing terms in the SGE bound smaller than
a fixed fraction of $\delta_1$. Note that the bias floor in Ineq.~\eqref{eq:sge-rate} is
$O(\mathcal{B}^2/\mu)$, condition \eqref{eq:cert-bias-condition}, with $c_0$ sufficiently small,
ensures
$
    \tfrac{\mathcal{B}^2}{\mu}
    \lesssim
    \tfrac{a\mu R^2}{S^2}
    =
    \delta_1,
$
and consequently $\mathbb{E}[\phi_{0}(\widehat x_{1}) - \phi^*_{0}] \leq \delta_{1}$.

Now consider $j\ge2$. Assume
$\widehat x_{j-1}$ is a $\delta_{j-1}$-approximate minimizer of
$\phi_{j-2}$, i.e., $\mathbb{E}[\phi_{j-2}(\widehat x_{j-1}) - \phi^*_{j-2}] \leq \delta_{j-1}$. Then Ineq.~\eqref{eq:rr-new-dist} indicates that the initial distance to the optimal solution
$
\mathbb{E}\|\widehat x_{j-1}-x_{j-1}^*\|^2
\le
\tfrac{\delta_{j-1}}{\rho_{j-1}},
$
and the initial optimality gap
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}[\phi_{j-1}(\widehat x_{j-1}) -\phi_{j-1}^*]
\le \mathbb{E}[\phi_{j-2}(\widehat x_{j-1}) -\phi_{j-2}^*]\leq {\delta_{j-1}},
\label{eq:initial_optimality_gap}
\end{equation}
In the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:rr-pg}, we show that the $j$-th subproblem $\phi_{j-1}$ is $\rho_j$-strongly convex and
has smoothness at most $2L$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:rr-noise}, the effective residual variance at this
level satisfies
\[
\mathbb{E}[\widehat\sigma_{j-1,*}^2]
\le
\sigma_*^2
+
\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\delta_i \le
\sigma_*^2
+
\tfrac{2a\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}\mu R^2}{S^2}.
\label{eq:cert-effective-variance}
\]
where the second inequality follows from \eqref{eq:cert-delta-choice}. By the first inequality in \eqref{eq:sge-rate} of Theorem~\ref{thm:sge}, we have
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[\phi_{j-1}(x_{k_j})-\phi_{j-1}^*]
\le &\mathcal{O}\left(\left(\tfrac{L}{k_j^2}+\tfrac{\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}}{mk_j^2}+\tfrac{\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}^2}{\rho_j m^2k_j^2}\right)\tfrac{\delta_{j-1}}{\rho_{j-1}}+ \tfrac{\delta_{j-1}}{k_j^2}+\tfrac{\sigma_*^2}{\rho_j  mk_j} + \tfrac{a \ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}\mu R^2}{\rho_jS^2 m k_j}+\tfrac{\mathcal{B}^2}{\rho_j }\right). 
\end{align*}
Note that $
    \tfrac{
       \delta_{j-1}
    }{\rho_{j-1}\delta_j}
    =
    \tfrac{4}{\rho_j}.
$ Therefore, with mini-batch size
$m=1$, it suffices to use
\begin{equation}
k_j
=
O\left(
\sqrt{\tfrac{L}{\rho_j}}
+
\tfrac{\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}}{\rho_j}
   
                          
+
\tfrac{S^2\sigma_*^2}{\mu^2R^2} + \tfrac{\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}}{\mu}
\right)
\label{eq:cert-j-th-budget}
\end{equation}
to make all vanishing terms (terms other than $\tfrac{\mathcal{B}^2}{\rho_j}$) smaller than a fixed fraction of $\delta_j$. Meanwhile, condition \eqref{eq:cert-bias-condition} suggests that, when $c_0$ is sufficiently small, the bias floor satisfies
$
    \tfrac{\mathcal{B}^2}{\rho_j}
    \lesssim
    \tfrac{a\mu^2R^2}{S^2\rho_j}
    =
    \delta_j.
$
As a consequence, we have $\mathbb{E}[\phi_{j-1}(\widehat x_{j}) - \phi^*_{j-1}] \leq \delta_{j}$, and the inductive argument is complete.

Now we check the total sample complexity. Summing up $k_j$ over all
$S=O(\log(L/\mu))$ recursive-regularization levels, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\sum_{j=1}^S k_j = \mathcal{O}\left(
    S\sqrt{\tfrac{L}{\mu}}
    +
    \tfrac{S\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}}{\mu}
+
\tfrac{S^3\sigma_*^2}{\mu^2R^2}
\right).
\end{align*}

It remains to prove the projected-gradient guarantee.
By Ineq.~\eqref{eq:RR_reduction} in Proposition~\ref{prop:rr-pg} and Ineq.~\eqref{eq:cert-delta-choice},
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\|\mathsf{G}_{X}(\widehat y)\|
\leq (2+\sqrt{2})\sum_{j=1}^{S-1}\sqrt{\rho_j\delta_j}
+
6\sqrt{\rho_S\delta_S}
=
\big((2+\sqrt{2})S + 4 -\sqrt{2}\big)\tfrac{\sqrt a\mu R}{S}
\leq 6
\sqrt a\mu R.
\end{aligned}
\]
Choosing $\sqrt{a}\le\sqrt{2}/96$ yields $\mathbb{E}\|\mathsf{G}_{X}(\widehat y)\|
    \le
    \tfrac{\sqrt{2}\mu R}{16}$, which proves the first inequality in Ineq.~\eqref{eq:cert-constant-prob}.
Finally, by using Markov's inequality, we have
$
\ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}\left(
  \|\mathsf{G}_{X}(\widehat y)\|
  >
  \tfrac{\sqrt{2}\mu R}{4}
\right)
\le
\tfrac{\sqrt{2}\mu R/16}{\sqrt{2}\mu R/4}
=
\tfrac14,
$
which proves the second inequality in Ineq.~\eqref{eq:cert-constant-prob} and completes the proof.
\end{proof}

iterations to make all vanishing terms in the SGE bound smaller than
a fixed fraction of $\delta_1$. Note that the bias floor in Ineq.~\eqref{eq:sge-rate} is
$O(\mathcal{B}^2/\mu)$, condition \eqref{eq:cert-bias-condition}, with $c_0$ sufficiently small,
ensures
$
    \tfrac{\mathcal{B}^2}{\mu}
    \lesssim
    \tfrac{a\mu R^2}{S^2}
    =
    \delta_1,
$
and consequently $\mathbb{E}[\phi_{0}(\widehat x_{1}) - \phi^*_{0}] \leq \delta_{1}$.

Now consider $j\ge2$. Assume
$\widehat x_{j-1}$ is a $\delta_{j-1}$-approximate minimizer of
$\phi_{j-2}$, i.e., $\mathbb{E}[\phi_{j-2}(\widehat x_{j-1}) - \phi^*_{j-2}] \leq \delta_{j-1}$. Then Ineq.~\eqref{eq:rr-new-dist} indicates that the initial distance to the optimal solution
$
\mathbb{E}\|\widehat x_{j-1}-x_{j-1}^*\|^2
\le
\tfrac{\delta_{j-1}}{\rho_{j-1}},
$
and the initial optimality gap
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}[\phi_{j-1}(\widehat x_{j-1}) -\phi_{j-1}^*]
\le \mathbb{E}[\phi_{j-2}(\widehat x_{j-1}) -\phi_{j-2}^*]\leq {\delta_{j-1}},
\label{eq:initial_optimality_gap}
\end{equation}
In the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:rr-pg}, we show that the $j$-th subproblem $\phi_{j-1}$ is $\rho_j$-strongly convex and
has smoothness at most $2L$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:rr-noise}, the effective residual variance at this
level satisfies
\[
\mathbb{E}[\widehat\sigma_{j-1,*}^2]
\le
\sigma_*^2
+
\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\delta_i \le
\sigma_*^2
+
\tfrac{2a\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}\mu R^2}{S^2}.
\label{eq:cert-effective-variance}
\]
where the second inequality follows from \eqref{eq:cert-delta-choice}. By the first inequality in \eqref{eq:sge-rate} of Theorem~\ref{thm:sge}, we have
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[\phi_{j-1}(x_{k_j})-\phi_{j-1}^*]
\le &\mathcal{O}\left(\left(\tfrac{L}{k_j^2}+\tfrac{\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}}{mk_j^2}+\tfrac{\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}^2}{\rho_j m^2k_j^2}\right)\tfrac{\delta_{j-1}}{\rho_{j-1}}+ \tfrac{\delta_{j-1}}{k_j^2}+\tfrac{\sigma_*^2}{\rho_j  mk_j} + \tfrac{a \ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}\mu R^2}{\rho_jS^2 m k_j}+\tfrac{\mathcal{B}^2}{\rho_j }\right). 
\end{align*}
Note that $
    \tfrac{
       \delta_{j-1}
    }{\rho_{j-1}\delta_j}
    =
    \tfrac{4}{\rho_j}.
$ Therefore, with mini-batch size
$m=1$, it suffices to use
\begin{equation}
k_j
=
O\left(
\sqrt{\tfrac{L}{\rho_j}}
+
\tfrac{\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}}{\rho_j}
   
                          
+
\tfrac{S^2\sigma_*^2}{\mu^2R^2} + \tfrac{\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}}{\mu}
\right)
\label{eq:cert-j-th-budget}
\end{equation}
to make all vanishing terms (terms other than $\tfrac{\mathcal{B}^2}{\rho_j}$) smaller than a fixed fraction of $\delta_j$. Meanwhile, condition \eqref{eq:cert-bias-condition} suggests that, when $c_0$ is sufficiently small, the bias floor satisfies
$
    \tfrac{\mathcal{B}^2}{\rho_j}
    \lesssim
    \tfrac{a\mu^2R^2}{S^2\rho_j}
    =
    \delta_j.
$
As a consequence, we have $\mathbb{E}[\phi_{j-1}(\widehat x_{j}) - \phi^*_{j-1}] \leq \delta_{j}$, and the inductive argument is complete.

Now we check the total sample complexity. Summing up $k_j$ over all
$S=O(\log(L/\mu))$ recursive-regularization levels, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\sum_{j=1}^S k_j = \mathcal{O}\left(
    S\sqrt{\tfrac{L}{\mu}}
    +
    \tfrac{S\ensuremath{\mathcal{L}}}{\mu}
+
\tfrac{S^3\sigma_*^2}{\mu^2R^2}
\right).
\end{align*}

It remains to prove the projected-gradient guarantee.
By Ineq.~\eqref{eq:RR_reduction} in Proposition~\ref{prop:rr-pg} and Ineq.~\eqref{eq:cert-delta-choice},
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\|\mathsf{G}_{X}(\widehat y)\|
\leq (2+\sqrt{2})\sum_{j=1}^{S-1}\sqrt{\rho_j\delta_j}
+
6\sqrt{\rho_S\delta_S}
=
\big((2+\sqrt{2})S + 4 -\sqrt{2}\big)\tfrac{\sqrt a\mu R}{S}
\leq 6
\sqrt a\mu R.
\end{aligned}
\]
Choosing $\sqrt{a}\le\sqrt{2}/96$ yields $\mathbb{E}\|\mathsf{G}_{X}(\widehat y)\|
    \le
    \tfrac{\sqrt{2}\mu R}{16}$, which proves the first inequality in Ineq.~\eqref{eq:cert-constant-prob}.
Finally, by using Markov's inequality, we have
$
\ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}\left(
  \|\mathsf{G}_{X}(\widehat y)\|
  >
  \tfrac{\sqrt{2}\mu R}{4}
\right)
\le
\tfrac{\sqrt{2}\mu R/16}{\sqrt{2}\mu R/4}
=
\tfrac14,
$
which proves the second inequality in Ineq.~\eqref{eq:cert-constant-prob} and completes the proof.

label: lem:block-counts
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:block-counts}
Under the SGE stage-cost \eqref{eq:stage-complexity}, we have
$
Q\le\binom{\ell}{2}.
$
head: environment
name: Economic switches

title: Proof
body_md:
From \eqref{eq:stage-complexity}, the stage cost of SGE has the form
$
C_k(\lambda)=\max\{\alpha_\lambda,\beta_\lambda2^k\}.
$
For any two oracles $\lambda$ and $\nu$, their strict ordering can change at most once as $k$ increases. 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
Thus one unordered stochastic oracle pair can trigger at most one strict economic switch. Since removed oracles never return to the pool, we have $Q\le\binom{\ell}{2}$.
head: environment

label: thm:budgeted-cost
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Cost of budgeted sparse certification

label: eq:successful_blocks
title: Proof
body_md:
First, note that the fully successful blocks cover disjoint certified level intervals. By \eqref{eq:block-vs-pg-switching}, every contraction stage in such blocks costs no more than the corresponding stage of our benchmark, while the cost of the PG stage is at most $\zeta$ times its SGE-equivalent stage cost by \eqref{eq:pg-cost-comparable}. Therefore, the single-trial stochastic-training cost of all fully successful blocks is at most $\zeta C_{\rm sw}^{\rm PG}$.\footnote{Here, we do not carefully distinguish the cost of the contraction stage and PG stage, as $\zeta$ is only a logarithmic factor of the condition number.}  Considering the sequential implementation rule with at most $\mathcal{R}$ trials, we have
\begin{align}\label{eq:successful_blocks}
    \mathrm{Cost}(\text{all fully successful blocks}) \leq \mathcal{R}\zeta C_{\rm sw}^{\rm PG}.
\end{align}

For a failed block, by the budget constraint rule in \eqref{eq:block-stop-budget}, the uncertified training cost of all contraction stages is at most $B$, as shown in Ineq.~\eqref{eq:block-budget}.  Meanwhile, in case $B$ is very large or even $\infty$, we can always bound the block's contraction cost by $C_{\rm sw}^{\rm PG}$ due to \eqref{eq:block-vs-pg-switching}. Therefore, the total cost of the contraction stages in all failed blocks is bounded by
\begin{align}\label{eq:failed_blocks}
    \mathrm{Cost}(\text{all contraction stages in all failed blocks}) \leq \mathcal{R}M \min\{B,  C_{\rm sw}^{\rm PG}\}= \mathcal{R}M \bar B.
\end{align}
                                                                                                                                                       

It remains to account for the terminal PG costs of failed blocks, i.e.,
\[
\mathrm{Cost}(\text{PG stages in all failed blocks})
=
\mathcal{R}\sum_{b\ {\rm failed}}
\widetilde C_{k_b}(\lambda_b),
\]
where $\lambda_b$ and $k_b$ are the oracle and terminal stage of failed block $b$. On the high-probability event under consideration, a removed oracle cannot be PG-admissible at its terminal stage: for the SGE/RR+SGE implementation, terminal PG-admissibility makes the whole block block-admissible, and Lemma~\ref{lem:block-validity} together with Proposition~\ref{prop:budgeted-correctness} rules out such a false rejection on this event. Thus $k_b\ge\kappa_{\lambda_b}$. Moreover, because $\lambda_b$ is selected at $k_b$ while the current pool contains an oracle attaining $C_{k_b}^\star$, we have 
$
C_{k_b}(\lambda_b)\le C_{k_b}^\star
$
by \eqref{eq:block-vs-pg-switching}.
Therefore the terminal PG cost of each failed oracle is bounded by its corresponding summand in \eqref{eq:bad-oracle-identification-cost}. Since each oracle can fail at most once, we have
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Cost}(\text{PG stages in all failed blocks})\le \mathcal{R}C_{\rm bad}^{\rm PG}.
\label{eq:elim-by-cbad}
\end{equation}

Finally, we need to compute the total certification cost. To do so, we need to count the successful certification blocks. If a fully successful block is terminated by the budget condition and its terminal stage is $t-1$, then
\[
\sum_{k=s}^{t-2}A_k(\lambda)+A_{t-1}(\lambda)>B.
\]
The corresponding successful block intervals are disjoint, and their total (single-trial) contraction subroutine cost is at most $C_{\rm sw}^{\rm PG}$ by \eqref{eq:block-vs-pg-switching}. Therefore, there are at most
$
\lceil C_{\rm sw}^{\rm PG}/B\rceil
$
budget-triggered successful blocks. In addition there are $Q$ economic-switch blocks and at most one final block, while the total number of successful blocks is at most $K$. Thus, the total number of successful blocks is bounded by $\min\left\{
K,\,
\left\lceil\tfrac{C_{\rm sw}^{\rm PG}}{B}\right\rceil+Q+1
\right\}$, and 
the total number of certification blocks is at most
$
\min\left\{
K,\,
\left\lceil\tfrac{C_{\rm sw}^{\rm PG}}{B}\right\rceil+Q+1
\right\}
+M,
$
indicating a total certification cost of
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Cost}(\text{all certification steps})\le \mathcal{R}c_{\rm cert}
\left[
\min\left\{
K,\,
\left\lceil\tfrac{C_{\rm sw}^{\rm PG}}{B}\right\rceil+Q+1
\right\}
+M
\right].
\label{eq:total_certification}
\end{equation}
Combining Ineqs.~\eqref{eq:successful_blocks}, \eqref{eq:failed_blocks},  \eqref{eq:elim-by-cbad}, and \eqref{eq:total_certification} proves Ineq.~\eqref{eq:budgeted-cost-first}.

title: Corollary
head: environment
name: U-shaped certification tradeoff

title: Proof
body_md:
For $B\le C_{\rm sw}^{\rm PG}$, we have $\bar B=B$ and
$
\lceil C_{\rm sw}^{\rm PG}/B\rceil
\le C_{\rm sw}^{\rm PG}/B+1.
$
Also recall the upper bound $M\leq \ell$ and $Q\leq \binom{\ell}{2}$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:block-counts}. 
 Applying these inequalities in \eqref{eq:budgeted-cost-first} yields \eqref{eq:budgeted-clean-U}. 
 By minimizing the two $B$-dependent terms, we can show $B^*$ and $\mathrm{Cost}_{B^*}$.
